\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Mr. Gray stated today they will be talking about the potential impacts on services. He explained the County's total budget is approximately $1.3 billion. At first glance, a potential $119 million reduction may appear to be relatively a small percentage of the total, but County revenues are not interchangeable. Much of the budget consists of revenues that are legally restricted for specific purposes. The three funds supported by property taxes have approximately $562 million in total revenues. Under the full implementation of Amendment 3, he estimates those funds would lose approximately $119 million in reoccurring revenue; and that is the challenge they are preparing for. He asked each department: If your available funding was permanently reduced by approximately 20%, what would that mean for the services that we provide to our residents and business owners? The presentations are the result of that question. Mr. Gray closed his opening statements by stating Seminole County is largely a service organization. The services are delivered and provided through people who are the employees that maintain roads and stormwater systems, librarians, park employees, animal service officers, firefighters, paramedics, and hundreds of other public servants who come to work every day to serve the community. That means a permanent revenue reduction of this magnitude will affect the workforce, and the impact would extend beyond County employees.\par
\par
Tim Jecks, Management and Budget Director, addressed the Board and presented the item as outlined in the agenda backup. Rick Durr, Parks and Recreation Director, addressed the Board and provided the Parks and Recreation Potential Budget Impacts slides. Commissioner Zembower stated as they dig deeper, there are cuts that they may be discussing that actually can't be cut on certain properties because of the way that the County came to those properties, so he would like to see that information. He also requested to see a breakdown over the last 10-15 years of State mandates and the costs associated with those. Tawny Olore, Public Works Director, addressed the Board and provided the Potential Budget Impacts slides for Roads, Bridges, Traffic, Engineering & Mass Transit. She reminded that the Board of County Commissioners does not have control over the tax levies or budgets of the School Board, the Water Management District, the Property Appraiser, Tax Collector, or any of the seven cities in Seminole County. Questions regarding assessed property valuations should be addressed to the Property Appraiser David Johnson, who is present.\par
\par
Mr. Gray stated tonight is the first of two public hearings on the FY 2026-2027 budget required by Florida statute. The purpose of tonight's hearing is to present the tentative budget for all funds and proposed millage rates for the Countywide District, the Fire MSTU, and the Road MSTU. This public hearing was advertised through the TRIM notice mailed to each property owner in August. The millage rates and budget considered for adoption tonight are the result of six budget work sessions. Mr. Gray reviewed a few of the budget highlights. He noted the budget is balanced. He commented while Amendment 3 if passed will not directly impact the FY 2026-2027 proposed budget, they believe it is important to begin those conversations sooner rather than later. Each Commissioner has received a detailed statement of the necessary adjustments, which is included in the public hearing document included in the agenda backup.\par
\par
Mr. Jecks presented the Tentative Budget Overview for FY 2026-2027. He advised the Tentative Budget is balanced with revenues and expenditures totaling $1.27 billion, which includes adjustment reductions of $13,405,476 from the proposed budget delivered to the Board in June. Mr. Jecks reviewed the First Public Hearing Revenue Adjustments and Expenditure Adjustments as detailed in the public hearing document in the agenda backup. \par
\par
Mr. Jecks advised the FY 2027 rates are the same as the current rates for all districts. The increase over the rolled back rate will be used to meet state-mandated obligations, maintain public safety services, and offset cost increases for transportation. He announced the tentative rates as follows: The general Countywide Millage of 5.3751 mills is 4.18% above the rolled back rate of 5.1595 mills. The Fire MSTU millage of 2.7649 mills is 4.06% above the rolled back rate of 2.6569 mills. The Unincorporated Roads MSTU millage of 0.1107 mills is 4.24% above the rolled back rate of 0.1062 mills. The Tentative Aggregate Millage Rate for all BCC taxing districts is 7.3620 mills which is 4.01% over the current aggregate rolled back rate of 7.0781 mills.\par
\par
With regard to public participation, Gabriella Mengel (document received and filed) and Gwynne Guthrie spoke in opposition to Automated License Plate Readers (Flock cameras); Leslie Grubl spoke and urged the public to review the budget work sessions that have been held, and she summarized the services that will be impacted if Amendment 3 passes; Eric Fiedler spoke on commercial property tax increases; Bill Hyde spoke on Save Our Homes; and John Horvath spoke on the budget.\par

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Mr. Gray stated this is the second part of the discussion on Amendment 3 potential service impacts. At the August 25th work session, they heard from Parks and Recreation, Public Works, Environmental Services, and Community Services about the potential funding reductions and what that could mean for services they provide to the community. Today they are turning the attention to Public Safety, which includes the Sheriff's Office, the Fire Department, Emergency Management, Emergency Telecommunications, and Animal Services. Management and Budget Director Tim Jecks will close with a discussion on Unfunded State Mandates.\par
\par
Of the $562 million in revenues within property tax-supported funds, approximately 72% currently supports Public Safety, 5% supports Unfunded Mandates, and 3% supports Constitutional Officers. The estimated Amendment 3 impact is 21% or $119 million. Those obligations and the projected revenue loss together exceed the revenues currently available in these funds. He previously brought department directors and division managers together and asked them to take a hard look at their operations and identify what a permanent 20% reduction in available funding could mean for staffing, programs, and services. He advised the Sheriff and his team went through the same exercise.\par
\par
Sheriff Dennis Lemma addressed the Board and discussed the potential budget impacts for the Sheriff's Office. He emphasized Amendment 3 does not provide exemptions for Public Safety. A 20% reduction represents approximately $41 million in annual operating revenue, which depends almost exclusively on funding appropriated by the County Commission. There is an important distinction in Amendment 3 that needs to be clearly understood. The amendment specifically excludes school district taxes from the increased homestead exemption, which means the revenue that funds schools is treated differently and is not subject to this reduction. There is no similar protection for Public Safety. There is a false narrative that suggests Amendment 3 offers protections for Public Safety; but there is no Public Safety exemption in Amendment 3, and it does not guarantee a minimum level of funding for any Public Safety services. While the amendment identifies Public Safety as one of the purposes for which remaining property tax revenue may be used, that is not the same as protecting or exempting Public Safety funding. There is no state funding in Tallahassee waiting to replace those local dollars should there be a significant loss of revenue. A reduction of approximately $41 million would compromise public safety. There were Board comments and questions.\par
\par
Mr. Jecks addressed the Board and reviewed the Fire Department Budget. Fire Chief Matt Kinley addressed the Board and presented the Fire Department Potential Budget Impacts slides. There were Board comments and questions. Mr. Jecks reviewed the Emergency Management budget. Alan Harris, Emergency Management Director, addressed the Board and presented the Emergency Management Potential Budget Impact slides. There were Board comments and questions. Mr. Jecks then presented and reviewed the Unfunded State Mandates slide. \par
\par
With regard to public participation, John Horvath and Leslie Grubl spoke.\par
\par
Written Comment Form with attached letter was submitted from Seminole County Professional Fire Fighters President Jon DiVita.\par
\par
No one else spoke and public input was closed.\par
\par
Public Comment Forms and Written Comment Form were received and filed.\par
}

Under discussion, Commissioner Dallari stated he has talked to staff and the applicant about a transmission line that goes through this piece of property. He didn't hear it today, and he wants to make sure they coordinate with FPL for any and all work in or around that transmission line. Chairman Herr noted for the record the applicant nodded in the affirmative.

action_text:
Motion by Commissioner Constantine, seconded by Chairman Herr, to find, based on Staff’s findings and the testimony and evidence received at the hearing, the request does not meet the following provisions of the LDC: Section 30.3.1.5(a)(1), (2) and (4); Section 30.6.17.5(5)(2) and (3); and Section 30.69.17.5 and moves to deny the Special Exception request for an existing civic assembly use to expand in the A-1 (Agriculture) and R-1AA (Single Family Dwelling) zoning districts on approximately 1.93 acres, located on the northwest corner of Citrus Street and Laura Avenue; Jain Society of Central Florida; Applicant; as described in the proof of publication.
Under discussion, there was lengthy Board discussion with few questions for the Applicant and staff.
Commissioner Constantine commented the applicant talked about 50 children for the second building, and he doesn't think they need 15,000 square feet for 50 children. There has to be an economy of scale that is balanced. For that reason, Commissioner Constantine amended the motion to deny without prejudice, so if they want to come back and redo this, in working with the community, scale it down, the Board will be able to entertain that without all of the costs of coming back. The seconder agreed.
Districts 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 voted AYE.
Upon Chairman Herr's inquiry if she had everything she needed, Neysa Borkert, Deputy County Attorney, clarified it is denied without prejudice so they can reapply, and there is no limit to time frame on when they can come back with the same special exception request but with a different site plan.
Chairman Herr recessed the meeting at 3:12 p.m., reconvening at 3:25 p.m.
